desc:
You have a list of tasks, where tasks[i] = [duration, deadline]. You start working at time 0, do one task at a time, never pause a task once it has started, and may do the tasks in any order you like. A task that starts at time s finishes at s + duration, and that finish time must be at most its deadline.

Return true if some order lets you finish every task on time, otherwise false.

tasks = [[3, 6], [2, 2], [1, 10]]  ->  true
tasks = [[2, 2], [1, 2]]           ->  false

In the first example do the second task (finish at 2), then the first (finish at 5), then the third (finish at 6). In the second example the work takes 3 time units but both deadlines are 2.
hints: The total amount of work never changes with the order. What does change is when each individual task finishes.
If a task with a late deadline is done before a task with an early deadline, could swapping the two ever make things worse?
Sort the tasks by deadline (earliest first), keep a running sum of durations, and check that the running sum never exceeds the deadline of the task just added.
editorial: Do the tasks in order of increasing deadline (earliest deadline first) and keep the finish time as a running sum. If the running sum ever exceeds the deadline of the current task, report false; if it never does, report true.

Why this order is enough: suppose some valid order has two neighbouring tasks A then B with deadline(A) > deadline(B). Swapping them makes B finish earlier and lets A finish exactly when B used to finish, which is not later than B's old finish and therefore not later than deadline(B) < deadline(A). So repeated swaps turn any valid order into the sorted one. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan is O(n).
